ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Right knee pain with clicking after increasing workouts; difficulty running longer distances for marathon training.
- Symptoms (onset/duration/severity/aggravating factors): Onset about 2 weeks ago, pain starts after ~20 minutes of running (around mile 2–3); pain worsens with flexion/extension exercises and long runs; occasional “giving way” sensation but not a full loss of stability; clicking with knee movements; transient swelling after the first run that resolved with ice; current knee not swollen and not painful at rest; able to fully straighten and flex the knee; pain mainly with activity (running/abs in gym).
- Associated features: Mid-knee pain with motion, occasional tingling in right toes after runs; no persistent redness, warmth, or fever; no difficulty walking normally; no locking sensation currently; no significant fatigue or systemic symptoms.
- Past medical history: Prior ice-hockey injury with a bruise several months ago; past acute UTI workup in ED (not directly relevant to current knee symptoms); generally good health otherwise; farsighted with prior LASIK; takes vitamin D; uses ibuprofen occasionally for joint discomfort; uses Aleve; uses melatonin; uses Xanax occasionally; smokes cannabis.
- Medications/allergies: Ibuprofen; Aleve (NSAIDs); Xanax (PRN); Melatonin; Vitamin D; Cannabis; No known drug allergies reported.
- Family/social history: Actively training for a marathon (distances increasing); high activity level; London resident; no smoking listed other than cannabis; no heavy alcohol use described.
- Vital signs/exam findings: Not provided in transcript; plan discussed included physiotherapy assessment and possible imaging if needed.
- Labs/imaging: None mentioned; referral to physiotherapist; discussion of possible knee imaging if swelling/heat/redness or locking develops; potential MRI if indicated after exam.
- Key negatives: No current knee locking; full ROM (can straighten and fully flex); no significant left knee issues; no obvious systemic illness.
- Red flags discussed: Possible concern for intra-articular pathology (cartilage/meniscal injury) or patellofemoral problems; patient worried about ligament injury (ACL) based on online info; doctor emphasized clinical assessment first and imaging if needed.

V: Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome (PAES) – exercise-induced leg pain behind the knee could be a vascular cause in a young athlete, though less likely given current presentation and absence of vascular symptoms.

Chronic exertional compartment syndrome (CECS) – leg pain with running and transient paresthesias could reflect increased intramuscular pressure during exercise, though knee-focused symptoms are more typical for other diagnoses.
I: Inflammatory or autoimmune arthropathy affecting the knee (e.g., inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis) – possible in adults with joint pain, though currently no systemic symptoms or morning stiffness described.
N: Osteoarthritis of the knee (degenerative) – age 45 and activity-related joint pain with mechanical symptoms is plausible.
Osteochondral lesion or loose body in the knee – can cause catching/clicking and intermittent pain with activity.
D: Meniscal tear (traumatic or degenerative) – classic for joint-line clicking, pain with activity, and intermittent effusion; aligns with onset after increased running.
Patellofemoral pain syndrome / chondromalacia patellae – common in runners; pain with knee bending, crepitus, and anterior knee pain related to loading activities.
Degenerative cartilage defects in the knee – overuse injuries or early degenerative changes could cause mechanical knee symptoms.
C: Congenital discoid meniscus – can cause mechanical symptoms (clicking, instability) though less likely at age 45; congenital variants can be asymptomatic until later in life or after overuse.
A: Autoimmune inflammatory arthritis (e.g., RA) – overlaps with category I; could present as monoarticular knee pain though less likely without systemic features.
T: Traumatic ligament injuries (e.g., ACL tear, MCL sprain) – history of a fall on ice and prior knee trauma could predispose to ligament injury, but current exam lacks instability or locking; still a possible etiology in the differential.
E: Endocrine/metabolic causes (e.g., metabolic bone/cartilage issues) – less likely given presentation, but metabolic bone health can affect joints over time.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Clicking with knee flexion/extension, pain emerging after several minutes of running, and a history of knee trauma/injury history fit a meniscal tear or degenerative meniscal change. Intermittent joint line discomfort and prior knee trauma support this. Absence of locking does not rule it out.
supporting_evidence: Clicking during flexion/extension of the knee
Pain beginning around mile 2–3 of running
Past knee injury with a prior knee bruise in ice hockey
Transient swelling after first run that resolved with ice
Ability to fully straighten and flex (ROM preserved)
opposing_evidence: No persistent locking or giving-way on exam
No definite focal joint-line tenderness described in transcript (requires clinical exam)

Pain localized around knee during activity without systemic symptoms
opposing_evidence: No explicit anterior knee pain or patellar grind described; imaging or exam needed to confirm
